Anand, twenty-four, was the newest clerk in the ward office. On Tuesday Divyansh, a senior colleague, put a hand on his shoulder. "Here we share the extras. Everybody chips in, everybody's safe." Anand said quietly that he would manage without.
By Friday nobody asked him to tea. Files piled onto his desk, and lunch was eaten in silence in the corner. He felt like a stranger in his own section.
The section officer called him in. "Keep every file note dated. If anyone pushes again, write it down and give it to me. I will send it to the vigilance cell." That afternoon she forwarded his note, and the cell acknowledged it within the day. Anand still felt lonely, but less afraid.

qa.q: How old was Anand?
qa.a: Anand was twenty-four.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling during the week after he said he would manage without?
qa.a: He felt lonely and like a stranger, with nobody asking him to tea and lunch eaten in silence.

qa.q: What made the difference in protecting Anand?
qa.a: The section officer told him to keep dated file notes, took his written note and forwarded it to the vigilance cell that afternoon, so a clear rule and a legal channel backed him.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have seen Anand's refusal?
qa.a: Divyansh may have felt uneasy or threatened, since he had called it a way everybody stays safe, and Anand's refusal broke that shared arrangement.

grounding: A young government employee is pushed to join a shared arrangement of favours, and refusing brings isolation but a mentor and legal channels protect them.

"You didn't come to the tea corner again," said Seema, setting her tray down opposite Kiran.
"I'm not in the mood."
"Because of the monthly 'collection' for the supervisor?"
Kiran looked at the table. "He said everyone contributes. I said no. Now I've been dropped from the office group and nobody speaks to me."

"It is lonely for a while. Write what was said, when and by whom. Dated. Then we take it to the chief this afternoon."

Kiran nodded, throat tight.

It was the peak of the monsoon, and the municipal office in Pune was flooded with building-permission files. Leela, twenty-five, three months into her first government job, was told by the senior clerk, "Everyone here takes a small 'tea share.' You'll get yours on Friday. Just sign where we tell you."
Leela didn't sign. On Friday, the envelope appeared on her desk. She pushed it back.
The next week, nobody invited her for lunch. Her files were "misplaced." She sat alone, the rain hammering the windows, wondering if she'd made a terrible mistake.
Karthik Sir, a section officer close to retirement, found her there one evening. "They did this to me too, in 1994," he said. "Keep a diary of every file and every instruction. Refuse politely. If they threaten you, go to the vigilance officer. I'll come with you."
Leela opened a notebook that night.

qa.q: What did Leela do when the envelope appeared?
qa.a: She pushed it back.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling as she sat alone?
qa.a: Leela felt lonely and doubtful, wondering if she'd made a terrible mistake by refusing.

qa.q: What made Karthik Sir's support protective?
qa.a: He shared his own experience, advised her to keep a diary and refuse politely, and offered to go with her to the vigilance officer.

qa.q: How might Karthik Sir feel seeing Leela refuse?
qa.a: Karthik Sir probably feels respect and a kind of recognition, remembering the same isolation in 1994.

grounding: A young government employee refuses to join colleagues' arrangement of favours, faces isolation, and finds protection in an honest mentor and legal channels.

Divyansh, twenty-four, joined the public works department as a junior engineer in Jaipur. In his second month, a contractor handed him a bill for road work that hadn't been done yet. "Sign it. Your senior already has. It's how we all eat," the contractor said.
Divyansh's hands went cold. He said he needed to inspect the road first.
Over the next week, his colleagues stopped greeting him. Someone left a note on his desk: "Don't be a hero."
He went to Hansa Ma'am, a senior engineer known for her strict honesty. She listened, then opened the department's rulebook. "You're right to inspect first. Write a note on the file saying the work isn't complete. Date it. Keep a copy." She added, "If they pressure you further, we go to the vigilance cell together."
Divyansh wrote the note that afternoon. His hands were still shaking.

qa.q: What did the note on Divyansh's desk say?
qa.a: It said, "Don't be a hero."

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when his hands went cold?
qa.a: Divyansh felt frightened and uneasy, pressured to sign for work that hadn't been done.

qa.q: How did Hansa Ma'am help protect Divyansh?
qa.a: She confirmed he was right, showed him the rules, told him to write and date a note on the file, and offered to go to the vigilance cell with him.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's colleagues see his refusal?
qa.a: They probably see it as a threat to their arrangement, which is why they stopped greeting him and left the note.

grounding: A young government engineer refuses to join colleagues' favours, faces isolation, and finds support from an honest mentor and clear rules.

"Samir, why haven't you signed the transfer list?"
"Harish-ji, three names on it don't meet the rules."
"They've paid. Everyone in the section shares. Your part is waiting."
"I don't want a part."
"You're new. Don't make enemies. It's how the office runs."
"Then the office runs wrong."
"Listen, beta, I'm telling you as a friend. Last year a boy like you refused. He was sent to a remote posting."
"Is that a threat?"
"It's advice."
"Then here's mine. I've written down which names don't meet the rules and why. I've sent a copy to the head of department, and I've kept one. If anything happens to me, it's on record."
Harish-ji stared. "You'll be very lonely here."
"Maybe. But I can sleep."

qa.a: Three names on it don't meet the rules.

qa.a: Samir probably feels threatened and uneasy, but determined, which is why he asks if it is a threat.

qa.a: He wrote down which names broke the rules and why, sent a copy to the head of department and kept one, putting it on record.

qa.a: Harish-ji seems surprised and uneasy, seeing Samir as a risk to the section's arrangement and warning him he'll be lonely.

passage: In my second month at the sub-registrar's office, the others made it clear there was a "system": a little extra from applicants who wanted their deeds registered quickly, shared out at the end of the week. On a Friday the head clerk slid an envelope across to me. "Your share, Dhruv. Don't be a hero." I pushed it back. After that, nobody called me for lunch. Files landed on my desk with pages missing. I felt very alone, and for a week I wondered if I'd been foolish. Then Irfan Sir, the senior deputy who'd been there nineteen years, took me for tea. "I refused too, long ago," he said. He gave me the vigilance department's number and the service rules on gifts, and told me to note down every envelope I saw. "Keep your papers clean and your notes dated. The rules protect you more than them." I still eat lunch alone some days. I sleep fine.

qa.a: He had been there nineteen years.

qa.a: Dhruv felt very alone and, for a week, wondered whether refusing had been foolish.

qa.q: What protections did Irfan Sir point Dhruv to?
qa.a: The vigilance department's number, the service rules on gifts, and keeping dated notes of every envelope seen.

qa.q: What might it mean to Irfan Sir to help Dhruv?
qa.a: Having refused too, Irfan Sir probably remembers that loneliness and feels glad to stand beside a newcomer making the same choice.
